heard: A giant star in our galaxy regularly chokes on its own soot. Discovered in 1795, the supergiant R. coroni borealis usually shines bright enough for the naked eye. But without warning, this reverse nova can plummet to nearly one millionth of its normal brightness. It doesn't explode outward like a typical star. Instead, it suddenly vanishes from view for months. Astronomers found the star is actually smothering itself in a massive cloud of carbon dust. Intense shockwaves force carbon gas to condense into thick, dark soot that blocks all visible light. While it disappears from our eyes, infrared telescopes can see right through the cosmic smog. Radiation pressure eventually clears the exhaust, revealing why this giant star regularly chokes on its own soot.
